sections.title: The Gateway: How did a sharpened stone become a smartphone?
sections.html:
Web address: /technology/stone-to-smartphone/ · Keywords: history of technology, how things work, types of technology, inventions timeline, technology for beginners

Technology is any tool or method people make to do something they could not do with bare hands: a stone flake that cuts, a wheel that rolls, a screw that holds, a chip that thinks. The phone in your pocket stands on about three million years of such steps, and on the work of millions of people whose names we will never know.

This short course asks one question in seven steps: how does technology grow, and how do the things around us actually work? It goes from the first stone tools to the wheel, the humble screw, electricity, the refrigerator and the internet, and ends with today's frontier. Each page takes about two minutes.

By the end you will be able to:

  • Say what the first technology was and how old it is.
  • Explain why the wheel came late.
  • Describe how a screw turns a twist into a grip.
  • Explain why electricity changed every other technology.
  • Describe how a fridge moves heat out of a box.
  • Trace a message from a server to your phone.
  • Name today's frontier technologies and their limits.

sections.title: What was the first technology?
sections.html:
Short answer: The oldest known tools are sharp stone flakes from Lomekwi, Kenya, about 3.3 million years old, older than our genus Homo. Control of fire, at least a million years ago, was the second great technology. India's own stone tools at Attirampakkam (Tamil Nadu) go back about 1.5 million years.

Keywords: first tool ever, Lomekwi stone tools, Oldowan, Acheulean handaxe, prehistoric technology India

Stone that cuts

Striking one stone with another breaks off a flake with an edge sharper than teeth. The Oldowan tools (about 2.6 million years ago, Olduvai Gorge) and the teardrop-shaped Acheulean handaxes (from about 1.76 million years ago) were used for a million years and more.

Fire, clothing, containers

Fire gave warmth, protection and cooked food (see COK). Needles of bone (about 40,000 years ago or earlier) gave sewn clothing (SEW). Pottery (about 20,000 years ago in China) gave cooking pots and storage.

Why it matters

Each tool made the next one possible. Archaeologists describe this as cumulative culture: humans learn from others and add improvements, so technology grows across generations.

Remember this: Technology is older than our species; it began with a sharp edge.

sections.title: Why did the wheel take so long to invent?
sections.html:
Short answer: The hard part was not the round wheel but the axle: a smooth pin that fits a hole in the wheel tightly enough to carry weight but loosely enough to turn. That needed metal tools and careful carpentry, so wheeled vehicles appear only about 3500 BCE, after farming, pottery and copper.

Keywords: invention of the wheel, history of the wheel, Ljubljana Marshes wheel, potter's wheel, wheel and axle

The evidence

  • Potter's wheel: Mesopotamia, about 4000 BCE or earlier.
  • Wheeled vehicles: pictures and models appear around 3500 to 3300 BCE from Mesopotamia to Central Europe; the Ljubljana Marshes wheel and axle (Slovenia) is about 5,150 years old.
  • India: toy carts of clay from Harappan sites and real solid-wheeled bullock carts; the spoked wheel came later and became the chakra of the Konark Sun Temple and the national flag.

Why late?

  • Axle fit: too tight and it jams; too loose and it wobbles.
  • Roads and animals: wheels need flat ground and draught animals.
  • No need: in the Americas, without horses or oxen, wheels appeared on toys but not carts.

Remember this: The wheel's genius is the axle, and that needed metal tools.

Next: Another simple machine hides in every piece of furniture. How does a screw hold?

sections.title: How does a screw hold things together?
sections.html:
Short answer: A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder. Turning it pushes it forward with great force, and the friction of its thread against the material holds it in place. That is why a small twist with a screwdriver can hold a heavy shelf.

Keywords: how screws work, screw simple machine, Archimedes screw, nut and bolt, fasteners

From pump to fastener

The screw as a machine is credited to Archimedes and others in the 3rd century BCE (the water-lifting Archimedes screw). Screw presses squeezed olives and grapes, and later printed books (TEC-08). Metal screws as fasteners became common only after machine-made threads in the 18th century.

Standard threads

Joseph Whitworth proposed a standard thread in 1841; later came metric (ISO) threads. Standards let a nut from one factory fit a bolt from another, a quiet revolution behind mass production.

Screws and their cousins

  • Wood screw: cuts its own thread.
  • Bolt and nut: clamp parts together.
  • Rivet: a permanent pin (aircraft, bridges).
  • Nail: holds by friction alone.

Remember this: A screw turns a gentle twist into a strong, lasting grip.

sections.title: Why did electricity change everything?
sections.html:
Short answer: Electricity turns energy from one place (a dam, a coal plant, a solar panel) into a form that travels instantly through wires and can become light, heat, motion, sound or information anywhere. Every later technology, from the fridge to the internet, depends on it.

Keywords: history of electricity, Faraday, Edison and Tesla, how electricity works, electrification of India

Key steps

  • 1800: Alessandro Volta's battery.
  • 1831: Michael Faraday discovers electromagnetic induction, the principle of every generator and transformer.
  • 1879: practical incandescent lamps by Thomas Edison and Joseph Swan.
  • 1880s and 1890s: the "current wars"; Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse's alternating current (AC) wins for long-distance supply.
  • India: Kolkata got electric street lighting in 1879 (demonstration) and public supply in 1899; Asia's early hydroelectric station at Sivasamudram, Karnataka (1902), powered the Kolar gold fields. India declared every village electrified in 2018.

What it unlocked

Lighting, motors, radio, refrigeration, computers and the grid itself. The US National Academy of Engineering ranked electrification the greatest engineering achievement of the 20th century (2000).

Remember this: Electricity is energy that can travel and transform.

sections.title: How does a fridge make cold?
sections.html:
Short answer: A fridge does not make cold; it moves heat out. A liquid refrigerant evaporates in pipes inside the fridge, soaking up heat (just as sweat cools your skin). A compressor then squeezes the vapour, and the coils at the back release that heat into the room as the refrigerant turns back into liquid.

Keywords: how a refrigerator works, vapour compression cycle, refrigerant, compressor, history of refrigeration

The cycle

  1. Evaporator (inside): low-pressure liquid boils and absorbs heat.
  2. Compressor: squeezes the gas, making it hot.
  3. Condenser (coils at the back): hot gas gives heat to the room and condenses.
  4. Expansion valve: pressure drops, and the cycle repeats.

A short history

Jacob Perkins patented a vapour-compression machine (1834); household fridges spread in the 1920s and 1930s. CFC refrigerants harmed the ozone layer and were phased out under the Montreal Protocol (1987); the Kigali Amendment (2016) phases down HFCs, which warm the climate.

The same idea, elsewhere

Air conditioners and heat pumps use the same cycle. India's traditional cooling, the clay matka and khus screens, works by evaporation too.

Remember this: A fridge is a heat pump: it carries heat from inside to outside.

sections.title: How does the internet reach your phone?
sections.html:
Short answer: Your message is split into small packets with addresses. They travel by radio to a mobile tower or Wi-Fi router, then through fibre-optic cables (including undersea cables) and routers to a data centre, and the reply comes back the same way, all in a fraction of a second. Common rules (TCP/IP) let different networks talk.

Keywords: how the internet works, packet switching, TCP/IP, undersea cables, 5G India

The building blocks

  • Packet switching: Paul Baran and Donald Davies (1960s); ARPANET (1969).
  • TCP/IP: Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn (1974); the internet adopted it on 1 January 1983.
  • World Wide Web: Tim Berners-Lee at CERN (1989 to 1991).
  • Fibre optics: light in glass; Narinder Singh Kapany's pioneering work (1950s) and Charles Kao's Nobel-winning insight (2009 prize).
  • Undersea cables: carry about 99 per cent of intercontinental data.

India online

Public internet arrived with VSNL on 15 August 1995. Cheap data after 2016, Aadhaar, UPI (2016) and 5G (from October 2022) made India one of the world's largest online populations.

Remember this: The internet is a network of networks sharing one set of rules.

sections.title: What is the newest technology today?
sections.html:
Short answer: As of November 2026, the fastest-moving fields are generative artificial intelligence, AI chips and data centres, renewable energy and batteries, gene editing and mRNA medicine, quantum computing, reusable rockets and brain-computer interfaces. Each is real but also surrounded by hype: check claims against peer-reviewed or official sources.

Keywords: latest technology 2026, emerging technologies, generative AI, quantum computing, brain computer interface

Frontier fields (dated, November 2026)

  • AI: large language models that write, code and reason; chip makers such as NVIDIA (its CEO Jensen Huang received the IEEE Medal of Honor, 2026).
  • Neural interfaces: the 2026 Queen Elizabeth Prize for Engineering honoured pioneers of cochlear implants and brain-computer interfaces.
  • Light-controlled neurons: the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine honoured optogenetics.
  • Quantum information: the 2025 Turing Award (announced 2026) went to Charles Bennett and Gilles Brassard for quantum cryptography.
  • Energy: cheap solar and batteries; India's target of 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030.
  • Space: reusable rockets, India's Chandrayaan-3 landing near the Moon's south pole (2023) and its first space docking (SpaDeX, 2025).

How to judge "new"

Ask: does it work outside the lab, at what cost, for whom, and with what risks?

Remember this: The frontier moves every year; this page is dated so you know when it was true.

parts.title: Trunk A: Electronic Devices and Home Appliances
parts.intro: About this Part. The devices of daily life. Each line says what it is, the idea behind it, who or when it began, and where it stands now. "Now" means November 2026; specifications change fast, so the website pages will carry dated details from manufacturers.

sections.title: Electronic devices
sections.html:
Before you start — TEC-02. Almost every electronic device rests on one invention: the transistor (Bell Labs, 1947, John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley), and on the integrated circuit (Jack Kilby, 1958; Robert Noyce, 1959) that packs billions of transistors on a chip. Gordon Moore observed in 1965 that the number doubled regularly ("Moore's law"); the pace has slowed but not stopped.

  • TEC-02.1 a Mobile phone: Martin Cooper's Motorola call (1973); India's first mobile call on 31 July 1995 (Jyoti Basu to Sukh Ram); smartphones from IBM Simon (1994) to the iPhone (2007) and Android (2008); India is the world's second-largest smartphone market and a major manufacturer.
  • TEC-02.1 b Tablet and e-reader: touchscreen slates; Kindle (2007) used E Ink (electronic paper that reflects light like print).
  • TEC-02.1 c Smartwatch and fitness band: sensors for steps, heart rate and sleep; accuracy varies and they are not medical devices unless certified.
  • TEC-02.1 d Wearables, AR and VR headsets: smart glasses, mixed-reality headsets; still searching for everyday uses.
  • TEC-02.1 e Calculator and pocket electronics: Texas Instruments' handheld (1967 prototype); a cheap calculator holds more computing than Apollo's guidance computer.

  • TEC-02.2 a Desktop PC: from the Altair (1975), Apple II (1977) and IBM PC (1981) to today's machines.
  • TEC-02.2 b Laptop: portable computers from the 1980s; India's affordable laptop schemes for students.
  • TEC-02.2 c Servers and data centres: buildings of computers that run the cloud and AI; huge users of electricity and water.
  • TEC-02.2 d Supercomputers: India's PARAM (C-DAC, 1991) and the National Supercomputing Mission; the world's fastest are listed twice a year on top500.org.
  • TEC-02.2 e Single-board computers: Raspberry Pi (2012) and Arduino microcontrollers (2005) for learning and making.
  • TEC-02.2 f Parts of a computer: CPU, GPU, memory (RAM), storage (hard disk, SSD), motherboard, power supply, input and output.

  • TEC-02.3 a Speakers and headphones: a coil moves a cone (the moving-coil loudspeaker, 1925, Rice and Kellogg); noise cancellation adds opposite sound waves.
  • TEC-02.3 b Microphones: dynamic, condenser and the MEMS microphones in phones.
  • TEC-02.3 c Television: John Logie Baird's mechanical TV (1926), electronic TV (Philo Farnsworth, Vladimir Zworykin); Doordarshan began in Delhi on 15 September 1959; colour in India from 1982 (Asian Games).
  • TEC-02.3 d Display technologies: CRT, LCD, LED-backlit, OLED, micro-LED; resolutions from HD to 8K.
  • TEC-02.3 e Projectors and monitors: DLP and LCD projectors; high-refresh monitors for gaming.

  • TEC-02.4 a Modem and router: the modem translates the line signal; the router directs traffic in the home.
  • TEC-02.4 b Wi-Fi: based on IEEE 802.11 (1997); CSIRO of Australia's patent was key; versions up to Wi-Fi 7.
  • TEC-02.4 c Mobile networks: 1G analogue to 5G; India's indigenous 4G and 5G stack by C-DOT and partners (BSNL rollout from 2024 to 2025).
  • TEC-02.4 d Fibre optics and switches: light pulses in glass carry the internet's backbone (TEC-00.06); BharatNet aims to connect every gram panchayat.
  • TEC-02.4 e Satellite internet: low-Earth-orbit constellations; licensing in India under the Telecommunications Act (2023).

  • TEC-02.5 a Batteries: Volta (1800), lead-acid (Gaston Planté, 1859), lithium-ion (Nobel in Chemistry 2019 to John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino); sodium-ion and solid-state are next.
  • TEC-02.5 b Chargers and power banks: USB-C is now the common standard (India moved new phones to it from 2025, in line with the EU).
  • TEC-02.5 c UPS and inverters: backup power, common in Indian homes.
  • TEC-02.5 d Solar inverters and rooftop solar: PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (2024) subsidises rooftop solar.

  • TEC-02.6 a Cameras: from the camera obscura (described by Ibn al-Haytham, about 1021) and photography (Niépce, Daguerre, 1820s to 1839) to the digital sensor (CCD, Boyle and Smith, 1969; Nobel 2009) and the CMOS sensors in phones.
  • TEC-02.6 b Drones: remote and autonomous aircraft for photography, mapping, farming (Namo Drone Didi scheme) and delivery; India's Drone Rules (2021).
  • TEC-02.6 c Gaming consoles: Magnavox Odyssey (1972) to today's consoles; see SPT for esports.
  • TEC-02.6 d Smart home and IoT: connected lights, plugs, cameras, speakers; the Matter standard (2022) for compatibility; privacy and security risks.

sections.title: Home appliances
sections.html:
Before you start — TEC-03. Appliances changed daily life, especially women's unpaid work, more than many famous inventions; the economist Ha-Joon Chang argued that the washing machine changed the world more than the internet (23 Things They Don't Tell You about Capitalism, 2010). India's Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) star labels (from 2006) help compare running costs.
  • TEC-03.1 Refrigerator: vapour-compression cycle (TEC-00.05); frost-free and inverter models; BEE star ratings.
  • TEC-03.2 Microwave oven: Percy Spencer noticed a melted chocolate bar near a radar magnetron (1945); microwaves shake water molecules to heat food.
  • TEC-03.3 Oven, OTG and air fryer: hot air and radiant heat; the air fryer is a small, fast convection oven.
  • TEC-03.4 Induction cooktop: a changing magnetic field heats an iron pan directly; efficient and safe, but needs magnetic cookware.
  • TEC-03.5 Mixer-grinder: India's kitchen workhorse; Sumeet (1963, designed by Satya Prakash Mathur) made it a household name for Indian wet grinding.
  • TEC-03.6 Pressure cooker: see COK-10.3c.
  • TEC-03.7 Washing machine: drum machines from the early 1900s; semi-automatic and fully automatic types; front- and top-loading.
  • TEC-03.8 Air conditioner: Willis Carrier (1902); inverter ACs and star ratings; refrigerants with lower warming potential.
  • TEC-03.9 Air cooler: evaporative cooling; works best in dry heat (Rajasthan), poorly in humid coasts.
  • TEC-03.10 Ceiling fan: Philip Diehl (1882); BLDC (brushless) fans use far less power.
  • TEC-03.11 Water purifier: filters, UV and RO (reverse osmosis); RO wastes water and removes minerals, so use it only where the water needs it (check TDS).
  • TEC-03.12 Geyser and water heater: storage, instant and solar water heaters.
  • TEC-03.13 Vacuum cleaner and robot vacuum: Hubert Cecil Booth's powered vacuum (1901); robot vacuums map rooms with sensors.
  • TEC-03.14 Electric iron: Henry Seeley's patent (1882); steam irons.
  • TEC-03.15 Lighting: incandescent, CFL, LED; India's UJALA scheme (2015) distributed over 36 crore LED bulbs.

parts.title: Trunk A: Mechanical Devices, Machines, Vehicles and Tools
parts.intro: About this Part. From the smallest fastener to the largest machines ever built. Mechanical technology is older than electronics and still holds the world together.

sections.title: Fasteners and simple machines
sections.html:
Before you start — TEC-04. Greek thinkers (Archimedes, Hero of Alexandria) listed the simple machines; Renaissance scientists settled on six. Each trades force for distance: you push less but farther. See also: TEC-00.03.
  • TEC-04.1 Lever: a bar on a pivot (fulcrum); seesaw, crowbar, scissors, the dhenkli well-sweep of Indian villages. "Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth" (attributed to Archimedes).
  • TEC-04.2 Wheel and axle: TEC-00.02; door knobs, steering wheels, the Persian wheel (rahat) for lifting water.
  • TEC-04.3 Pulley: a wheel with a rope; well pulleys, cranes, lifts.
  • TEC-04.4 Inclined plane: a ramp; how pyramids and temple towers were likely raised.
  • TEC-04.5 Wedge: two inclined planes back to back; axe, knife, chisel, plough.
  • TEC-04.6 Screw: an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder (TEC-00.03).
  • TEC-04.7 Fasteners: screws, nuts and bolts, nails (hand-forged, then machine-cut and wire nails), rivets, pins, washers, clips, zippers (Whitcomb Judson, 1893; Gideon Sundback's modern zip, 1913), Velcro (George de Mestral, 1955).
  • TEC-04.8 Gears, cams, springs and bearings: gears transmit turning force (the Antikythera mechanism, about 100 BCE, is the oldest known geared device); ball bearings reduce friction.
  • TEC-04.9 Locks and keys: Egyptian wooden pin locks (about 4,000 years ago), Linus Yale Jr's pin-tumbler lock (1860s), Aligarh's lock industry, today's smart locks.
  • TEC-04.10 Clocks: sundials and water clocks (ghati in India); the mechanical escapement (China's Su Song, 1090s; European clocks, 14th century); Christiaan Huygens's pendulum clock (1656); quartz (1927) and atomic clocks; India's time is kept by CSIR-NPL, New Delhi.

sections.title: Engines, vehicles and giant machines
sections.html:
• TEC-05.1 Steam engine: Thomas Newcomen (1712), James Watt's separate condenser (1769); the power of the Industrial Revolution.
  • TEC-05.2 Internal combustion engine: Nikolaus Otto's four-stroke (1876), Rudolf Diesel (1890s); now being replaced in many uses by electric motors.
  • TEC-05.3 Electric motor: Faraday's rotation (1821); motors drive fans, trains, EVs and robots.
  • TEC-05.4 Turbines and jet engines: steam turbine (Charles Parsons, 1884), jet engines (Frank Whittle and Hans von Ohain, late 1930s).
  • TEC-05.5 Bicycle: Karl Drais's running machine (1817), the chain-driven "safety bicycle" (John Kemp Starley, 1885); India's Atlas and Hero made it the people's vehicle.
  • TEC-05.6 Cars: Karl Benz's Motorwagen (1885 to 1886); Ford's Model T assembly line (1913); Maruti 800 (1983) put India on wheels; electric vehicles and the FAME and PM E-DRIVE schemes.
  • TEC-05.7 Trains: Stephenson's Rocket (1829); India's first passenger train, Bori Bunder to Thane (16 April 1853); Vande Bharat trains (2019) built at ICF Chennai; metros in many cities; the Mumbai–Ahmedabad high-speed rail under construction.
  • TEC-05.8 Ships and submarines: dhows and the Indian Ocean trade, steamships, container ships (Malcolm McLean, 1956); India's indigenous aircraft carrier INS Vikrant (commissioned 2022).
  • TEC-05.9 Aircraft: the Wright brothers (17 December 1903); India's first commercial flight, J. R. D. Tata from Karachi to Bombay (15 October 1932); HAL's Tejas light combat aircraft.
  • TEC-05.10 Rockets: Tipu Sultan's iron-cased Mysorean rockets (1780s and 1790s) inspired Britain's Congreve rockets; Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, Robert Goddard (first liquid-fuel rocket, 1926); India's first rocket launch from Thumba (21 November 1963); reusable boosters today.
  • TEC-05.11 Cranes, excavators and tunnel-boring machines: from Roman treadwheel cranes to TBMs that dug the Gotthard Base Tunnel (57 km, 2016) and India's Atal Tunnel (9 km, 2020, built by drill and blast).
  • TEC-05.12 The largest machines ever built: the Large Hadron Collider (27 km ring, CERN, 2008); the Bagger 293 bucket-wheel excavator; container ships of about 400 m; the International Space Station (from 1998).

sections.title: Tools and instruments
sections.html:
• TEC-06.1 Hand tools: hammer, screwdriver, spanner (wrench), pliers, saw, chisel, file, drill; the Indian basula (adze) and randa (plane) of the carpenter.
  • TEC-06.2 Power tools: electric drill (Wilhelm Fein, 1895; Black & Decker's pistol grip, 1917), angle grinder, circular saw, jigsaw, cordless tools.
  • TEC-06.3 Measuring instruments: ruler, vernier caliper (Pierre Vernier, 1631), micrometer, spirit level, multimeter, thermometer (Galileo's thermoscope; Fahrenheit and Celsius scales), barometer (Torricelli, 1643), weighing scales; the SI units (redefined in 2019).
  • TEC-06.4 Scientific instruments: microscope (Leeuwenhoek's single-lens microscopes, 1670s), telescope (Galileo, 1609), spectroscope; India's observatories (Jantar Mantar, Jaipur, UNESCO 2010).
  • TEC-06.5 Farm tools: plough, sickle, hoe (kudal), khurpi, seed drill (the Babylonian seed plough; India's bamboo seed drill, tifan; Jethro Tull's drill, 1701), threshers, tractors (India is the world's largest tractor maker by volume).
  • TEC-06.6 Craft tools: the loom, spinning wheel (charkha), potter's wheel, needles and hooks (CRO, KNT, EMB, SEW).

sections.title: Textiles and clothing technology
sections.html:
• TEC-07.1 Fibres: natural (cotton, first spun in the Indus valley; silk, China; wool; jute; linen), regenerated (rayon, viscose) and synthetic (nylon, Wallace Carothers at DuPont, 1935; polyester, 1941).
  • TEC-07.2 Spinning: hand spindle, charkha, the spinning jenny (Hargreaves, 1764), water frame (Arkwright, 1769), mule (Crompton, 1779), ring and rotor spinning.
  • TEC-07.3 Weaving: handlooms, the flying shuttle (John Kay, 1733), power loom (Cartwright, 1785), the Jacquard loom (1804), whose punched cards inspired early computers.
  • TEC-07.4 Dyeing and printing: indigo, madder, the Indian chintz and kalamkari traditions that astonished Europe; synthetic mauve (William Perkin, 1856).
  • TEC-07.5 Smart and technical textiles: conductive and sensor fabrics, fire-resistant and medical textiles; India's National Technical Textiles Mission (2020).
  • TEC-07.6 The sewing machine and knitting machine: Elias Howe (1846) and Isaac Singer (1851); William Lee's stocking frame (1589). See SEW and KNT.

sections.title: Printing, books and art technology
sections.html:
• TEC-08.1 Writing materials: clay, palm leaf (Indian manuscripts), birch bark, papyrus, parchment, paper (Cai Lun, China, 105 CE, by tradition).
  • TEC-08.2 Printing: woodblock printing (China; the Diamond Sutra, 868 CE), movable type (Bi Sheng, 1040s; Korea's metal type), Gutenberg's press (about 1450); India's first press at Goa (1556); Serampore Mission Press (1800).
  • TEC-08.3 Modern printing: lithography, offset, digital printing, 3D printing (Charles Hull's stereolithography, 1984).
  • TEC-08.4 Art technology: pigments (ochre, Indian yellow, lapis ultramarine), oil paint, paint tubes (John Rand, 1841), canvas, photography, digital art and drawing tablets, generative AI images (with debates about artists' consent and copyright). See BOK and MOV.
sections.summary: -  TEC-08.1 Writing materials: clay, palm leaf (Indian manuscripts), birch bark, papyrus, parchment, paper (Cai Lun, China, 105 CE, by tradition).

sections.title: Construction, transport and energy
sections.html:
• TEC-09.1 Construction materials: mud brick, fired brick (Harappan standardised bricks), lime mortar, Roman concrete, iron and steel (Delhi's rust-resistant iron pillar, about 400 CE), Portland cement (1824), reinforced concrete.
  • TEC-09.2 Architecture and structures: arches, domes and trusses; stepwells; skyscrapers (Home Insurance Building, Chicago, 1885); bridges (India's Chenab rail bridge, the world's highest railway arch bridge, opened 2025).
  • TEC-09.3 Transport systems: roads and highways (Grand Trunk Road; the Golden Quadrilateral, 2001 to 2012), railways, ports, airports, traffic signals and FASTag.
  • TEC-09.4 Energy: firewood to coal, oil, gas, nuclear (India's three-stage programme of Homi Bhabha; Tarapur, 1969), hydro, solar (Bhadla Solar Park, Rajasthan), wind, green hydrogen (National Green Hydrogen Mission, 2023), the grid (One Nation One Grid, 2013).

sections.title: Agriculture, food, water and sanitation
sections.html:
• TEC-10.1 Agriculture technology: irrigation, the plough, the Green Revolution's high-yield seeds, tractors, drip irrigation, soil health cards, drones, precision farming. See GRD.
  • TEC-10.2 Food technology: preservation, canning, refrigeration, pasteurisation (Louis Pasteur, 1860s), the cold chain, milk processing (Amul and Operation Flood), packaging, food fortification. See COK.
  • TEC-10.3 Water: stepwells and tanks, dams, canals, water treatment (chlorination from 1900s), desalination, Jal Jeevan Mission (2019) tap connections.
  • TEC-10.4 Sanitation: Harappan drains (among the world's earliest), the flush toilet (John Harington, 1596; Alexander Cumming's S-bend, 1775), sewers, twin-pit toilets, Swachh Bharat Mission (2014); Bindeshwar Pathak's Sulabh toilets (1970).

sections.title: Medical technology
sections.html:
Before you start — TEC-11. Medical technology is the long list the brief asks for. Every medical claim on the website will cite peer-reviewed reviews or regulators (WHO, CDSCO, US FDA). This index gives information, not medical advice.
  • TEC-11.1 Diagnostics: stethoscope (René Laennec, 1816), thermometer, blood pressure cuff (Riva-Rocci, 1896), lab tests, rapid tests, ECG (Willem Einthoven, Nobel 1924), pulse oximeter (Takuo Aoyagi, 1970s), point-of-care devices.
  • TEC-11.2 Imaging: X-rays (Wilhelm Röntgen, 1895; first Nobel in Physics, 1901), ultrasound, CT (Godfrey Hounsfield and Allan Cormack, Nobel 1979), MRI (Paul Lauterbur and Peter Mansfield, Nobel 2003), PET, AI-assisted reading of scans. Note: India's PCPNDT Act bans sex determination by ultrasound.
  • TEC-11.3 Surgery: anaesthesia (1846), antisepsis (Joseph Lister, 1867), Sushruta's ancient descriptions of rhinoplasty, laparoscopic (keyhole) surgery, robotic surgery, lasers.
  • TEC-11.4 Prosthetics and implants: the Jaipur Foot (P. K. Sethi and Ram Chandra Sharma, 1968), artificial joints, pacemakers (1958), cochlear implants (QEPrize 2026), stents, brain-computer interfaces.
  • TEC-11.5 Pharmaceuticals: aspirin (1897), insulin (1921 to 1922), penicillin (Fleming, 1928; mass-produced in the 1940s); India as the "pharmacy of the world" for generic medicines.
  • TEC-11.6 Vaccines: smallpox vaccination (Edward Jenner, 1796; variolation earlier in India, China and Africa), polio vaccines (Salk, Sabin), mRNA vaccines (Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, Nobel 2023); India's Covaxin and Covishield; Serum Institute of India, the world's largest vaccine maker by doses.
  • TEC-11.7 Telemedicine and digital health: eSanjeevani (2019), the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (2021), CoWIN.
  • TEC-11.8 Medical devices for hospitals: ventilators, dialysis machines (Willem Kolff, 1943), incubators, oxygen concentrators, radiotherapy.
  • TEC-11.9 Neurotechnology: EEG, deep brain stimulation, optogenetics (Nobel 2026, Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel).

sections.title: Communication, computing and AI
sections.html:
• TEC-12.1 Communication: drums and smoke signals, postal systems (India Post, 1854), the telegraph (Samuel Morse, 1837 to 1844; India's Calcutta–Diamond Harbour line, 1851), telephone (Alexander Graham Bell, 1876; Antonio Meucci earlier), radio (Marconi; J. C. Bose's millimetre-wave work, 1895), television, satellites, the internet, mobile.
  • TEC-12.2 Computing: the abacus, Indian decimal place value and zero (Brahmagupta, 628 CE), Charles Babbage's engines and Ada Lovelace's notes (1843), Alan Turing (1936), ENIAC (1945), the transistor, the microprocessor (Intel 4004, 1971), personal computers, the cloud.
  • TEC-12.3 Software: operating systems (Unix, 1969; Linux, 1991), programming languages (FORTRAN, C, Python), open source, India's IT services industry (TCS, 1968; Infosys, 1981; Wipro).
  • TEC-12.4 Artificial intelligence: the term coined at Dartmouth (1956); expert systems; machine learning; deep learning (the 2018 Turing Award to Yoshua Bengio, Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun; Hinton and John Hopfield's Nobel in Physics, 2024); AlphaFold (Nobel in Chemistry 2024 to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper, with David Baker); large language models and generative AI; the IndiaAI Mission (2024).
  • TEC-12.5 Quantum computing and quantum information: qubits, quantum cryptography (Turing Award 2025 to Charles Bennett and Gilles Brassard); India's National Quantum Mission (2023).
  • TEC-12.6 Cybersecurity: passwords and two-factor authentication, encryption, CERT-In, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023).

sections.title: Space, defence and materials
sections.html:
• TEC-13.1 Space: Sputnik (1957), Gagarin (1961), Apollo 11 (1969); ISRO (1969) under Vikram Sarabhai; Aryabhata (1975), SLV-3 (1980), INSAT, PSLV, Chandrayaan-1 (2008, water on the Moon), Mangalyaan (2014, Mars orbit on the first attempt), Chandrayaan-3 (2023), Aditya-L1 (2024), SpaDeX docking (2025), Shubhanshu Shukla on the International Space Station (Axiom-4, 2025); Gaganyaan human spaceflight in preparation; NavIC navigation.
  • TEC-13.2 Defence technology: from bows and wootz steel to gunpowder, radar, missiles; India's DRDO (1958), the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme under A. P. J. Abdul Kalam (1983), BrahMos, Agni, Tejas, Akash. Presented as history and engineering, not as weapons advice.
  • TEC-13.3 Materials: copper, bronze and iron ages; wootz (crucible) steel of South India, prized as "Damascus steel"; plastics (Bakelite, 1907); semiconductors (silicon); composites, graphene (isolated 2004; Nobel 2010), superalloys; India's semiconductor mission (2021) and first chip fabs.

sections.title: Biotechnology, environment, finance, education, entertainment and assistive technology
sections.html:
• TEC-14.1 Biotechnology: fermentation, the DNA double helix (1953), recombinant DNA (1973), PCR (Kary Mullis, 1983), the Human Genome Project (2003), CRISPR gene editing (Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier, Nobel 2020); India's Bt cotton (2002), Genome India project, Biocon.
  • TEC-14.2 Environmental technology: pollution control, catalytic converters, air-quality monitors, waste-to-energy, recycling, carbon capture, e-waste processing; India's E-Waste (Management) Rules (2022).
  • TEC-14.3 Financial technology: coins (India's punch-marked coins), paper money, banks, ATMs (1967; India's first, HSBC Mumbai, 1987), credit cards, online banking, UPI (NPCI, 2016; over 20 billion transactions a month by 2025), RuPay, digital rupee pilots, Aadhaar-enabled payments; risks: fraud and scams.
  • TEC-14.4 Education technology: the blackboard, printed textbooks, radio and TV classes (SITE 1975), MOOCs, SWAYAM (2017), DIKSHA, AI tutors; the digital divide.
  • TEC-14.5 Entertainment technology: cinema (MOV), recorded sound (MUS), radio, TV, video games (SPT), streaming, VR.
  • TEC-14.6 Assistive technology: Braille (Louis Braille, 1824; Bharati Braille for Indian scripts), white canes, hearing aids, screen readers, wheelchairs, sign-language apps; India's Accessible India Campaign (2015) and ADIP scheme.

parts.intro: About this Part. Inventors, engineers, companies and institutions. Many inventions had several fathers and mothers; we name the main ones and note disputes.

sections.title: Inventors and engineers
sections.html:
• TEC-18.1 a Aryabhata and Brahmagupta: mathematics that underlies computing.
  • TEC-18.1 b Jagadish Chandra Bose (1858 to 1937): millimetre-wave radio experiments (1895), crescograph; refused to patent his early work.
  • TEC-18.1 c M. Visvesvaraya (1861 to 1962): engineer of the Krishna Raja Sagara dam and automatic flood gates; Bharat Ratna 1955; his birthday, 15 September, is Engineers' Day.
  • TEC-18.1 d Homi Bhabha and Vikram Sarabhai: founders of India's nuclear and space programmes.
  • TEC-18.1 e Satish Dhawan, U. R. Rao and K. Sivan: ISRO leaders; the Sriharikota launch centre is named after Dhawan.
  • TEC-18.1 f A. P. J. Abdul Kalam (1931 to 2015): SLV-3 project director, missile programme leader, President of India; Bharat Ratna 1997.
  • TEC-18.1 g Narinder Singh Kapany (1926 to 2020): "father of fibre optics"; Padma Vibhushan 2021 (posthumous).
  • TEC-18.1 h Sam Pitroda, Nandan Nilekani and the India Stack team: C-DOT telephone exchanges; Aadhaar and digital public infrastructure.
  • TEC-18.1 i Ajay Bhatt and Vinod Dham: co-inventor of USB at Intel; a key engineer of the Pentium chip.
  • TEC-18.1 j Women in Indian technology: Tessy Thomas ("Missile Woman", Agni), Ritu Karidhal and M. Vanitha (Chandrayaan and Mangalyaan), Roddam Narasimha's colleagues, Kalpana Chawla (astronaut), Sudha Murty (Telco's first woman engineer).
  • TEC-18.1 k Grassroots innovators: the National Innovation Foundation (2000) and Anil Gupta's Honey Bee Network; Mansukh Prajapati's Mitticool clay fridge; Arunachalam Muruganantham's low-cost sanitary-pad machine; Saidullah's amphibious bicycle. Jugaad (frugal improvisation) is celebrated, with a note that it should not replace safety.

  • TEC-18.2 a Archimedes, Hero of Alexandria, Zhang Heng, Al-Jazari: ancient and medieval engineers; Al-Jazari's Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices (1206).
  • TEC-18.2 b Leonardo da Vinci: notebooks of machines, most never built.
  • TEC-18.2 c James Watt, George Stephenson, Isambard Kingdom Brunel: steam, railways, ships.
  • TEC-18.2 d Michael Faraday, Nikola Tesla, Thomas Edison, Alexander Graham Bell, Guglielmo Marconi: the electrical age.
  • TEC-18.2 e The Wright brothers, Henry Ford, Karl Benz, Bertha Benz (who made the first long car journey, 1888).
  • TEC-18.2 f Ada Lovelace, Alan Turing, Grace Hopper, John von Neumann: computing.
  • TEC-18.2 g Hedy Lamarr: co-inventor of frequency hopping (1942), an idea behind later wireless systems.
  • TEC-18.2 h Vint Cerf, Bob Kahn, Tim Berners-Lee: the internet and the Web.
  • TEC-18.2 i Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, Bill Gates, Linus Torvalds: personal computing and open source.
  • TEC-18.2 j Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun, Yoshua Bengio, Fei-Fei Li, Demis Hassabis: modern AI.

sections.title: Philosophy of technology
sections.html:
• TEC-20.1 Tools as extensions of the body: Ernst Kapp (1877) and Marshall McLuhan's Understanding Media (1964): "the medium is the message"; the wheel extends the foot, the book the eye.
  • TEC-20.2 Gandhi on machines: Hind Swaraj (1909) criticised machinery that displaced people; later Gandhi welcomed machines that served people, such as the Singer sewing machine; the charkha as a symbol of self-reliance.
  • TEC-20.3 Appropriate technology: E. F. Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful (1973), drew on Gandhian ideas; intermediate technology for villages.
  • TEC-20.4 Is technology neutral?: Langdon Winner's "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" (1980); Heidegger's "The Question Concerning Technology" (1954); Lewis Mumford.
  • TEC-20.5 Technological determinism versus social shaping: does technology drive society, or society shape technology? Most historians now say both.

sections.title: Technology and society
sections.html:
• TEC-21.1 Technology and jobs: the Luddites (1811 to 1816), automation, AI and work; studies differ on how many jobs will change; new skills and social protection.
  • TEC-21.2 Privacy and surveillance: data protection, India's Supreme Court ruling that privacy is a fundamental right (Puttaswamy, 2017), the DPDP Act (2023).
  • TEC-21.3 E-waste and the environment: the Global E-waste Monitor (2024) counted about 62 million tonnes of e-waste in 2022, with under a quarter documented as recycled; mining for critical minerals; energy use of data centres.
  • TEC-21.4 Repair culture and right to repair: repair cafés; the EU's right-to-repair rules; India's Right to Repair portal (2022) under the Department of Consumer Affairs.
  • TEC-21.5 Digital well-being: screen time, attention and sleep; WHO guidance for young children's screen time (2019); notification hygiene.
  • TEC-21.6 The digital divide and inclusion: access by gender, region and income; Indian-language interfaces; accessibility.
  • TEC-21.7 AI ethics and safety: bias, misinformation and deepfakes, copyright, safety research; India's IT Rules amendments on synthetic media; the EU AI Act (2024).
  • TEC-21.8 Psychology of technology: the "uncanny valley" (Masahiro Mori, 1970), the endowment effect with gadgets, variable rewards in apps, technostress.

sections.title: Choosing, caring for and recycling devices
sections.html:
• TEC-22.1 How to choose a device: decide your needs first; compare BEE star labels, warranty, service network, repairability and software-update years; read independent reviews with test data.
  • TEC-22.2 Care: keep vents clear, avoid heat, charge with certified chargers, update software, clean dust; descale geysers and kettles.
  • TEC-22.3 Electrical safety: earthing, MCBs and RCCBs (residual-current breakers save lives), ISI-marked wiring, never touch switches with wet hands, unplug during storms.
  • TEC-22.4 Battery safety: do not puncture or overheat lithium batteries; use proper chargers; dispose of them at collection points.
  • TEC-22.5 Cyber safety: strong passwords and a password manager, two-factor authentication, never share OTPs, report fraud at cybercrime.gov.in or helpline 1930.
  • TEC-22.6 Right to repair and recycling: use authorised e-waste collectors (CPCB list); donate working devices; remove personal data before giving away.
  • TEC-22.7 Learning technology: maker spaces, Atal Tinkering Labs in schools (2016), online courses, electronics kits, coding clubs.
  • TEC-22.8 Careers: engineering branches, ITI trades, diploma courses, research, design, repair entrepreneurship.
